authors: Omar Vasquez Duque
title: The Magical Number 2 (Minus Two): An Empirical Analysis on the Efficacy of Choice Screens to Increase Competition in Digital Markets
venue: Working paper (draft 2025-07-17), NYU School of Law; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026
method: matrix completion (causal panel estimator, related to synthetic control/DiD) on monthly StatCounter country panel, EU countries vs non-EU high-income donor pool, 2017-early 2025, bootstrap CIs
outcomes: Google Search mobile market share; Chrome mobile browser share
headline: DMA choice screens lowered Google's EU mobile search share by about 0.56 points (95% CI -0.71 to -0.39) and Chrome's share by about 1.80 points (95% CI -2.20 to -1.41).
summary_plain: After the DMA forced phones in the EU to show choice screens, Google's and Chrome's market shares fell, but only by about half a point and two points. The author concludes choice screens barely dent dominant positions.
period_geography: 2017-early 2025; EU member states vs non-EU high-income countries
quality: Causal panel design with explicit counterfactual; StatCounter page-view data is a noisy proxy; single-author draft, not peer reviewed.

authors: Joan Calzada, Néstor Duch-Brown, Xavier Fageda, Nicandro Quirós
title: Who benefits from Google's SERP? The impact of the DMA on the Air Travel Market
venue: Working paper (Universitat de Barcelona / JRC), January 2026; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026
method: difference-in-differences on domain-level Similarweb traffic data, four EU countries vs UK and US controls, Nov 2023-Dec 2024
outcomes: organic search, direct and referral web traffic to airline and flight comparison websites
headline: Google's DMA-driven search page redesign raised organic search traffic to low-cost airlines by 14-28% on desktop and 8-22% on mobile, and to smaller flight comparison sites by up to 28.9%, with no significant change for Skyscanner or Booking.com.
summary_plain: When Google removed its own Google Flights box from EU search results to comply with the DMA, more people clicked through to smaller airlines and smaller flight comparison sites. Big airlines and big comparison sites saw little change.
period_geography: Nov 2023-Dec 2024; four EU countries vs UK and US
quality: Credible DiD with pre-trend checks; Similarweb traffic estimates are modelled; one sector; one co-author at the Commission's JRC.
interested_party: One co-author is employed by the European Commission (JRC)

authors: Victorine Verlooy, Monty Lukas Meier, Vincent Heimburg, Maximilian Schreieck
title: The Impact of the EU's Digital Markets Act: An Event Study
venue: ECIS 2025 Proceedings (European Conference on Information Systems), paper ECIS2025-1916
method: event study of gatekeeper stock returns around DMA announcement and implementation events
outcomes: investor reactions (abnormal stock returns of gatekeepers)
headline: Gatekeeper stocks reacted positively to DMA regulatory announcements, but this optimism faded during the implementation stage (abstract gives no magnitudes).
summary_plain: Investors initially reacted well to news about the DMA, perhaps expecting more competition and value, but that reaction faded once the rules had to be put into practice.
period_geography: DMA announcement to implementation (approx. 2020-2024); listed gatekeeper firms
quality: Standard event-study design; small number of firms and events; abstract only, magnitudes not seen.

authors: Matthias Bauer, Dyuti Pandya (ECIPE)
title: What About Us? Consumer Response to the Digital Markets Act
venue: ECIPE Occasional Paper, October 2025
method: survey of 3,500 consumers (500 each in 7 Central and Eastern European countries), Ipsos online panel, July 2025, quota sampled; descriptive statistics
outcomes: consumer-reported friction, privacy concern, platform usage, DMA awareness
headline: 39% of respondents report needing more steps for tasks that used to be simple, about one-third find online services less seamless since DMA changes, and 80% are unfamiliar with the DMA.
summary_plain: A survey of consumers in seven Central and Eastern European countries found many people say online services became more cumbersome after DMA changes, while most still rely on Google and Meta and few know the law exists.
period_geography: July 2025; Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania
quality: Self-reported perceptions, no counterfactual; attribution to the DMA rests on respondents; authors recommend repealing the DMA.
interested_party: Survey commissioned by EPPP; ECIPE states support from industry partners; authors advocate repeal or reform of the DMA

authors: Nextrade Group (for CCIA Europe)
title: Impact of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) on consumers across the European Union: Results from a survey with 5,000 consumers
venue: Nextrade Group report, September 2025
method: online survey of 5,000 consumers in 20 EU member states, 28 April-15 May 2025; descriptive statistics
outcomes: consumer-reported search time, service quality, personalisation, willingness to pay for pre-DMA services
headline: Two-thirds of respondents say they now have to search longer than before the DMA; 35% report worse map services and 42% of frequent travellers say flight and hotel results are less helpful.
summary_plain: An industry-commissioned survey of 5,000 Europeans found most say finding things online got slower and less convenient after the DMA, and many would like the old services back.
period_geography: April-May 2025; 20 EU member states
quality: Recall-based perceptions without counterfactual; question framing attributes changes to the DMA; commissioned by an industry body.
interested_party: Commissioned by CCIA Europe (trade association whose members include gatekeepers)

authors: Jane Choi (Analysis Group)
title: What Happens to App Prices when Developers Pay Lower Commission Fees? Evidence from the European Union
venue: Analysis Group study, November 2025 (hosted by Apple)
method: before-after comparison of prices 90 days before and after enrolment in Apple's DMA alternative business terms, ~21,000 apps/in-app purchases, 41m+ transactions; no control group
outcomes: App Store prices; pass-through of commission cuts; distribution of savings
headline: Despite commission rates falling about 10 percentage points, developers kept prices the same or raised them on 91% of products; more than 86% of the EUR 20.1m in savings went to non-EU developers.
summary_plain: When Apple cut its fees for EU apps under the DMA, app makers mostly did not lower prices for users; they kept the savings, and most of the money went to developers outside the EU.
period_geography: March-September 2024 enrolment cohorts; EU App Store storefronts
quality: Descriptive before-after design without control group; Apple data; does not cover alternative marketplaces.
interested_party: Funded by Apple, a designated gatekeeper

authors: Dirk Auer (ICLE)
title: The Commission's Seven Claims, Tested
venue: International Center for Law & Economics
method: structured qualitative assessment of the seven core claims in the Commission's April 2026 DMA review, against published evidence
outcomes: contestability, consumer welfare, user data control, legal certainty
headline: Argues the Commission's evidence of DMA success (e.g. 250% more Aloha browser users, Firefox iOS users doubling in Germany and France) is vendor-reported input counts without a counterfactual, and that net consumer-welfare effects are mixed and for several provisions likely negative.
summary_plain: A critical think-tank scorecard of the Commission's own DMA review: it says the Commission counts activity (new app stores, more browser downloads) rather than real benefits to users and ignores costs.
quality: Structured critique, no new data; relies on selected secondary studies; strongly critical prior position.
interested_party: ICLE is a long-standing DMA critic and receives funding from technology companies

authors: Javier Delgado (Mirai)
title: DMA implementation sinks 30% of clicks and bookings on Google Hotel Ads
venue: Mirai blog, May 2024
method: comparison of Google Hotel Ads click volumes for 3,450 hotels in DMA vs non-DMA markets, 1 Jan-22 Apr 2024 (difference-style comparison, no formal model)
outcomes: Google Hotel Ads clicks and direct hotel bookings
headline: Google Hotel Ads clicks fell about 30% in DMA-affected markets relative to non-DMA markets in the three months after Google's DMA changes.
summary_plain: A hotel booking-technology firm found that after Google changed EU search results for the DMA, hotels got about 30% fewer clicks from Google's hotel ads compared with markets outside the EU.
period_geography: Jan-Apr 2024; EU vs non-EU markets, 3,450 client hotels
quality: Simple treated-vs-control comparison on a vendor's client base; short window; no statistical testing reported.
interested_party: Mirai sells hotel direct-booking and metasearch services

authors: Pablo Delgado (Mirai)
title: DMA impact on hotels: 0.8% loss of direct reservations
venue: Mirai blog, October 2024
method: before-after comparison (8 months either side of 19 Jan 2024) of Google Analytics 4 booking attribution for 3,000+ hotels, EU vs non-EU
outcomes: share of direct hotel bookings by source (Google Hotels, Ads, organic, metasearch)
headline: Google Hotels' share of EU hotels' direct bookings fell from 13.4% to 8.9%; after partial recapture via other channels, the net loss of direct reservations was about 0.8%.
summary_plain: Using booking data from over 3,000 hotels, the firm found the DMA changes cut bookings coming via Google's hotel box, but hotels won most of this back through other Google channels, for a net loss of under 1% of direct bookings.
period_geography: May 2023-Sept 2024; EU vs non-EU markets
quality: Descriptive share comparison on vendor client base; attribution-model dependent; no statistical inference.
interested_party: Mirai sells hotel direct-booking and metasearch services

authors: Maria del Sorbo, Carina Faber, Marco Grazzi, Francesco Matteucci, Miriam Ruß
title: Assessing changes in EU innovation policy programs: from SME instrument to EIC accelerator for start-up funding
venue: Economia e Politica Industriale: Journal of Industrial and Business Economics 53(2): 501-537 (2026); earlier DISCE working paper dipe0037 (2024)
method: applicant-data comparison of selection (probit-type funding determinants) plus regression discontinuity on evaluation scores for the EIC Accelerator pilot
outcomes: applicant profile; funding determinants; patenting, revenue and employment growth
headline: The EIC Accelerator pilot attracted younger, smaller and more high-tech firms than the SME Instrument, but RDD estimates of funding effects on patenting, revenue and employment are not statistically significant given the short post-period.
summary_plain: The EU's start-up funding scheme now reaches younger, more high-tech companies than its predecessor, but it is still too early to show that the money made those firms grow faster.
period_geography: SME Instrument (2014-2020) and EIC Accelerator pilot (2018-2020) applicants; EU and associated countries
quality: Strong RDD design but underpowered; covers the Horizon 2020 pilot that became Horizon Europe's EIC Accelerator (predecessor instrument); authors include EIC staff.
interested_party: Two or more authors work for the European Innovation Council (European Commission)

authors: PPMI, IDEA Consult, UNU-MERIT for European Commission DG RTD
title: To what extent are Widening countries part of knowledge networks formed by the framework programmes? Working paper supporting the interim evaluation of Horizon Europe (support study on Excellent Science)
venue: Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2777/2418909
method: dynamic network analysis of participation and collaboration networks in FP7, Horizon 2020 and early Horizon Europe (centrality, hub analysis)
outcomes: Widening countries' participation and collaboration shares, network centrality
headline: Widening countries show an increasing trend in collaboration shares into Horizon Europe, but large member states still steer consortia, few network hubs sit in Widening countries, and Hungary's share fell while Poland, Romania and Bulgaria stayed low.
summary_plain: A study for the Commission finds that lower-performing EU countries are slowly becoming better connected in EU research projects under Horizon Europe, but big Western countries still run most of the networks.
period_geography: FP7 (2007-2013), Horizon 2020 (2014-2020), Horizon Europe (2021-early 2024); EU and associated countries
quality: Descriptive network statistics, no causal identification; supports the Commission's own interim evaluation.
interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission (DG RTD)

authors: Veronica Orsanigo, Thomas Louf, Eleonora Andreotti, et al.
title: Collaboration, Integration, and Thematic Exploration in European Framework Programmes: A Longitudinal Network Analysis
venue: arXiv:2604.11339 (physics.soc-ph)
method: longitudinal country-level collaboration network analysis of CORDIS data for all nine Framework Programmes (FP1-Horizon Europe) plus semantic embeddings of project descriptions
outcomes: network integration of countries; thematic breadth of funded research
headline: Across all nine FPs including Horizon Europe, collaboration progressively integrates marginal countries but core-periphery asymmetries persist, and research exploration (117 topics) is more focused than a random benchmark.
summary_plain: Looking at 40 years of EU research programmes up to Horizon Europe, the authors find EU projects slowly pull newer member countries into research networks, but the core-periphery divide has not closed.
period_geography: 1984-2025 (FP1 to Horizon Europe projects starting before end-2025); EU and associated countries
quality: Descriptive; Horizon Europe is only the latest of nine programmes covered, no causal claims; preprint.

authors: European Court of Auditors
title: Annual reports concerning the 2024 financial year, Chapter 5 'Competitiveness for growth and jobs' (research: Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe)
venue: European Court of Auditors, October 2025
method: statistical audit sample of 99 research transactions (65 Horizon 2020, 34 Horizon Europe); error-rate estimation
outcomes: regularity of spending (error rates), adaptation to simplified rules, uptake of lump-sum funding
headline: Quantifiable errors in 26 of 99 research transactions, with no significant difference between Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe despite simplification; lump sums were only about 15% of grants signed in 2024 against a 50% target by 2027.
summary_plain: EU auditors found that Horizon Europe's simpler cost rules have not yet reduced mistakes in how research money is claimed, and that the simplest funding method (lump sums) is used far less than planned.
period_geography: 2024 financial year; EU
quality: Rigorous audit sample, but small Horizon Europe subsample (34) and focused on compliance rather than research outcomes.

authors: European Commission
title: Annual Report on Research and Technological Development Activities of the European Union and Monitoring of Horizon Europe in 2025
venue: European Commission (summarised by EISMEA IP Helpdesk, 31 May 2026)
method: programme monitoring statistics (proposals, grants, participants, reported outputs)
outcomes: participation, funding, SME share, innovation outputs and patents
headline: By end-2025 Horizon Europe had awarded EUR 52.8bn through 19,456 grants to over 31,000 organisations; SMEs were 35% of participants and projects reported 7,645 innovations and 94 patent applications.
summary_plain: The Commission's monitoring report counts how much Horizon Europe money has gone out and to whom, and early outputs such as new products and patent applications.
period_geography: 2021-2025; EU and associated countries
quality: Descriptive self-reported monitoring, no counterfactual; seen only via an official EU agency summary, not the report itself.
interested_party: Commission reporting on its own programme

authors: Thomas Conlon, Shaen Corbet, Les Oxley
title: The influence of European MiCa regulation on cryptocurrencies
venue: Global Finance Journal 63 (2024), doi:10.1016/j.gfj.2024.101040
method: event study of crypto-asset returns around MiCA-related announcements
outcomes: crypto-asset returns by asset type
headline: Announcement-day returns fell by about 2.1% around MiCA announcements, persisting up to three days, with stronger effects for digital assets, platform tokens and utility tokens.
summary_plain: Crypto prices dipped by about 2% on days when news about the EU's MiCA rules came out, especially for some token types.
period_geography: MiCA legislative milestones (approx. 2020-2023); global crypto markets
quality: Standard event study of announcements (legislative stage, not application); headline taken from the search-engine abstract snippet, publisher page blocked, metadata confirmed via Crossref/Unpaywall.

authors: Chiara Drolsbach, Nicolas Pröllochs
title: Content Moderation on Social Media in the EU: Insights From the DSA Transparency Database
method: descriptive analysis of 156 million Statements of Reasons in the DSA Transparency Database over two months
outcomes: frequency, grounds, automation and type of moderation decisions by platform
headline: TikTok made more than 350 times more moderation decisions per user than X/Twitter; most decisions were automated, while X reported relying solely on manual methods.
summary_plain: Using the EU's new database of platform moderation decisions, the authors found platforms report in very different ways, which suggests the DSA is being applied unevenly.
period_geography: Sept-Nov 2023; EU, eight very large social media platforms
quality: Large-scale measurement of self-reported data; early window; no causal design.

authors: Daria Dergacheva, Vasilisa Kuznetsova, Rebecca Scharlach, Christian Katzenbach
title: One Day in Content Moderation: Analyzing 24 h of Social Media Platforms' Content Decisions through the DSA Transparency Database
venue: Lab Platform Governance, Media and Technology (ZeMKI), University of Bremen, technical report
method: descriptive analysis of one day of Statements of Reasons from eight VLOP social media platforms in the DSA Transparency Database
outcomes: volume, automation and categories of moderation decisions
headline: The eight platforms reported over 2 million moderation decisions in one day, about 68% automated, while X declared no automated decisions at all.
summary_plain: A snapshot of one day of data that big platforms must send to the EU shows millions of moderation decisions, mostly automated, and big inconsistencies between how platforms describe them.
period_geography: One day in autumn 2023 (with checks on 4 and 10 Oct); EU
quality: One-day snapshot, descriptive; useful early compliance evidence only.

authors: Benedetta Tessa, Gautam Kishore Shahi, Amaury Trujillo, Stefano Cresci
title: When Transparency Falls Short: Auditing Platform Moderation During a High-Stakes Election
venue: EPJ Data Science (2026), doi:10.1140/epjds/s13688-026-00704-8; arXiv:2604.19285 (earlier version arXiv:2504.06976)
method: time-series analysis of 1.58 billion self-reported moderation actions in the DSA Transparency Database by eight largest platforms over eight months around the 2024 European Parliament elections
outcomes: changes in moderation volume and strategy around elections; data quality
headline: Across 1.58 billion moderation actions, platforms' self-reported enforcement patterns did not change significantly around the 2024 European Parliament elections, and transparency gaps persisted a year after the database launched.
summary_plain: Platforms did not visibly change how they moderated content around the 2024 EU elections, according to the data they must report under the DSA, and that data still has big gaps.
period_geography: Eight months around June 2024; EU
quality: Large-scale interrupted-time-series style measurement; relies on self-reported data whose structure may hide changes.

authors: Amaury Trujillo, Benedetta Tessa, Stefano Cresci
title: Disarranged Harmonization of Transparency Reporting by Social Media Platforms Under the Digital Services Act
method: large-scale quantitative data-quality analysis of transparency reports and database submissions of the eight largest platforms after the Commission's harmonised reporting templates, plus structured comparison
outcomes: compliance and data quality of DSA transparency reporting (formatting, timeliness, consistency, completeness)
headline: After the Commission's harmonisation rules, all eight platforms still showed problems in data formatting, timeliness, consistency and completeness, and some submitted contradictory information across reporting channels.
summary_plain: Even after the EU standardised how platforms must report their moderation, the reports remain messy, late or inconsistent, making them hard to check.
period_geography: 2025-2026; EU, eight largest social media platforms
quality: Systematic measurement of compliance; no causal design; preprint.

authors: Marie-Therese Sekwenz, Ben Wagner, Hans De Bruijn
title: From Reports to Reality: Testing Consistency in Instagram's Digital Services Act Compliance Data
venue: ACM Journal on Responsible Computing (doi:10.1145/3821526); arXiv:2507.01787
method: multi-level consistency analysis of Instagram's DSA compliance data (transparency reports, database, other disclosures); case study
outcomes: consistency of DSA compliance reporting
headline: A multi-level consistency framework applied to Instagram's DSA reporting can detect potential compliance failures across interconnected reporting channels (abstract gives no headline numbers).
summary_plain: By cross-checking the different reports Instagram must publish under the DSA, the authors show inconsistencies that can flag possible compliance failures.
period_geography: 2023-2024; EU, Instagram
quality: Single-platform case study; method-focused; abstract lacks quantitative results.

authors: Adriana Mutu, L. Pătraș
title: TikTok, child safety, and the Digital Services Act: An empirical analysis of online harm mitigation
venue: Communications (De Gruyter), 2026, doi:10.1515/commun-2025-0120
method: descriptive and cross-tabulation analysis of 11.6 million TikTok Statements of Reasons from the DSA Transparency Database at four time points in 2024-2025
outcomes: TikTok moderation actions for protection of minors
headline: Across 11.6 million TikTok moderation records, content flagged under 'Protection of Minors' is a significant share of moderation activity.
summary_plain: TikTok's own DSA reports show that a large part of what it removes or restricts is flagged as harmful to children.
period_geography: Four snapshots 2024-2025; EU, TikTok
quality: Descriptive, single platform, self-reported data; abstract seen via Semantic Scholar metadata.

authors: Manuel Tonneau, Diyi Liu, Ryan McGrady, Kevin Zheng, Ralph Schroeder, Ethan Zuckerman, Scott A. Hale
title: Language Disparities in Moderation Workforce Allocation by Social Media Platforms
venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency (FAccT 2026), doi:10.1145/3805689.3806484
method: cross-platform audit of human moderator staffing by language using DSA-mandated transparency report disclosures, six platforms, relative to content volume
outcomes: moderator coverage and workload by EU language
headline: DSA disclosures reveal large cross-language disparities: millions of EU users on smaller platforms such as X post in languages with no dedicated human moderators, and per-moderator daily decision volumes differ by more than an order of magnitude across languages.
summary_plain: Using staffing data platforms must publish under the DSA, the study finds content in some languages gets far less human moderation than English, leaving some users less protected.
period_geography: 2023-2025 DSA transparency reports; EU, six major platforms
quality: Novel use of DSA transparency data; descriptive; depends on accuracy of self-reported staffing numbers.

European Health Data Space: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Act applies mainly from 2027-2029, so little ex-post evidence is likely. Needs a follow-up pass.
EuroHPC JU Regulation: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Needs a follow-up pass.
Critical Raw Materials Act: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Needs a follow-up pass (think tanks such as Bruegel and the Kiel Institute likely relevant).
Net-Zero Industry Act: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Needs a follow-up pass.

Connecting Europe Facility: not searched separately; shared web-search budget exhausted. The ECA 2024 annual report (Chapter 5) notes only 2 quantifiable errors in CEF transactions within a 28-transaction 'other programmes' sample, too thin to list. Needs a follow-up pass.
Single Market Programme: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Needs a follow-up pass.
Compulsory licensing of patents Regulation: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Adopted 2025 and no licence yet reported, so ex-post evidence is unlikely to exist.
STEP: not searched; shared web-search budget exhausted. Needs a follow-up pass.
